title: Life in the French Quarter, then Dick Richardson's band, Craig and Jackson
summary: Roommate life with Snoozer Quinn visiting, losing the Werlein job, the Dick Richardson band and Wingy, Oklahoma City, Francis Craig in Nashville, and settling in Jackson in 1945.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: What was the name of the restaurant?

I can't remember, but it was just almost directly across the street. It was in the 327, close to where the Royal Semester is now. And I lived at the Pontaubo building as soon as I got a salary, and had another close friend at Royal Arms who was in the refrigerator department, the name was Bennett D's. And then I shared 519, we lived at 519 St. Henn, first floor apartment, $45 a month. He paid $22.50 and I paid $22.50. And he was a great bathtub gin mixer, and we had lots of fun. Snoozer used to come down and play for me. We'd, we had a deck chair, had a little banana tree, it was really, it had some fine atmosphere. And Snoozer would play just as long as we'd hand him a drink. He'd just play for me. Sidney Ayrton, the guy who wrote Lazy River, used to come down. Cause they all liked to come down. They didn't have access to, to those things too much. And we were really living just fine. I'd get up in the morning and just walk straight up the street to the Royal Arms, you know, enter on the back side, on the Charlotte Street side, and go to work. And, and just a few blocks home, you know, no traffic problem, no nothing. Just, I enjoyed it very much. But, all good things have to come to their name sometimes. So, uh, Elmo Gogeti, who is 45, was with Werleins, 45 years, had been running Collins Pianicone, which was actually owned by Werleins, and under a different name. And so, they closed them up. And so, Gogeti, they had to make a place for Gogeti. So, uh, they brought Gogeti over and gave him the job I had, and put me back on a straight permission arrangement. And by this time, I was about ready to go back playing anyway. So, I had an offer to go to Beaumont and play with Pat and Bob Dequeer. And in a band called the New Orleans. And, uh, and from there, I played about a year that time, I guess. And, uh, after that, I went on, that's when I went back to Strayport, and, uh, to join. And, uh, it's a Dick Richardson band, really. But, Dean Kincaid was the arranger. Yank Lawson was one of the trumpeters. Wenge was one of the trumpeters. Roger Boyd, who is one of the really great drummers. He's dead now, he was one of them. In fact, this band was terrific. It was just wonderful. We rehearsed all day long. We had boom syringes, which were very modern at that time. And, uh, so, we were supposed to open at a new nightclub in Strayport, called The Castle. But, they, the man who actually had the hiring of the band, had charged the hiring of the band, was Paul English. Paul English was a famous, tense show man. He had had, uh, wonderful dramatic stock companies, and, uh, traveled all over Louisiana. This was a popular thing, they did dramatic shows at that time. But, he was a showman all the way through. So, we were sitting there, starving, and rehearsing, and waiting to go into the castle. He went to Kansas City, and he heard a band called the Taurus Brothers. They had three changes of uniform. They played all kinds of Latin music, and, uh, just a show band out of the world. So, he came back, said, boys, I'm real soft. But, I just had to hire the first time. There was just so much to attract people. Of course, all we did was play jazz, and good arrangements, and everything. So, I never will forget. But, Wingy and I were living at the Buckhoff Hotel, and, uh, Wingy, I was trying to handle, uh, porch out from the Wingy. And, I never will forget, uh, I saw Wingy got coming out when I pulled up some years. I don't remember what's going on. And, uh, next morning, Wingy was gone. He had caught a train. A freight train. With that one arm, to Chicago. And, uh, he had connections in Chicago. He had always worked in Chicago. And, uh, but, Wingy, just to give you an idea how good this band was, Wingy would hitchhike to Dallas, trying to book this band under its own name. And, of course, the most success I can cause was Dallas at all, the man of band. But, this was a really unusual jazz band for the time. And, uh, so, uh, we, uh, we came back and we couldn't book anything. And, so that, the reason for him to catch the freight train in Chicago, and then all the guys went different directions after that. And, then, we broke up. But, I had a chance to go to the Pumifus concert with, uh, up in England. And, I had a chance to go to Jenkins Music Company and work for my old boss in Oklahoma City. And, uh, Nick, this is the truth. I had, uh, I had a gold con alto sax. And, uh, I hadn't really get to it. I didn't want to call on my first school. So, I hocked my alto sax for ten dollars. And, I caught a bus. And, this is the truth. I caught a bus. At that time, you could ride a bus for a penny a mile. And, it was roughly 400 miles to Oklahoma City from Troop. And, so, uh, I landed in the sweep in, uh, Oklahoma City without a saxophone, but with my friend there and the job is to Jenkins Music Company. And, uh, I think I had to go to my college. And, uh, but I got started wonderfully in, uh, Oklahoma City and played with the very best bands. And, worked in the band department at the daytime, so I was, uh, getting on the plan. And, that's when Bernice and I were married in 1934. But, anyway, that's, this thing can go on and on. Um, I, I, I tell you, the best known name band I played with, I guess, was, uh, Francis Craig's band in Nashville. He played with better bands, but none better known. But, he had, uh, with Luke Needy and all those things. He had a real fine band. He'd been at the Hermitius Hotel for 25 years. So, I, I actually came from Wichita in 1943 to, uh, join John Gordy, where Papa John Gordy made a lot of records. He was, uh, he was a long-time friend of mine. We played together over in Elvira, Arkansas in the 20s, and he had been with Craig 20 years. He really ran the band. Craig just came down, you know, kicked off and wagged the stick, waved the stick. But, uh, anyway, I played with Craig for a time. And, at that time, I was on the camp shows with Minnie Ferrell and I did Pardews and all the present opera stars, the older ones at that time. And, but I didn't mind, really. We played, uh, Sewanee, Castle Heights. We played at the real room of the hotel at noon and for dinner. Then we'd pack up and go and play, uh, maybe Columbia, military school, maybe Sewanee, or just around all that territory. So, I got home to a three-a-ponk and I had been too long, a routine, self-aware. I mean, this didn't suit me very well. So, I decided I'd better get back to New York, so. And, uh, so I went on back to Wichita. Again, the job that I had, I could have caught on, but I didn't, uh, choose to bump another guy off. So, the company transferred me on up to Topeka Canyon, which I was where I was for a year. And then, Armie Brown, who I had met in the thirties with the Herbie Holmes Band, had come back to Jackson, Mississippi. And he and I had become good friends in Wichita. And so, he had organized this music store here in Jackson. And, um, he started corresponding with me when he'd come back. And when he got his store up to the point where he felt like he could afford another person in life, he made me a little girl up. And I came down here and stayed a week to be sure that I could, that I felt like I could fit back into the South. And, uh, so I came here in 1945, and I've been here ever since. So, I guess on that note, that would be a good thing to, a good time to stop boring you with all this history.
